From a CV to a resume: what I cut, and why it hurt

career
writing
Turning six years of academic work into one page for industry meant deleting most of what I was proud of. Here is what survived and the rules I used.
Published

September 17, 2026

The academic CV I defended with ran to four pages. The resume I now send runs to one, and almost nothing on it is phrased the way the CV phrased it. This post is the record of that conversion, written mostly so I remember the rules next time.

The CV describes what I studied. The resume describes what I built.

The first bullet on my old CV said I “synthesized 20 years of video-recorded interviews into a novel dataset examining the linguistic predictors of empathy in interpersonal conversation.” Every word is true and none of it tells a hiring manager what I can do for them. The replacement says what happened, in order: six legacy studies consolidated, 74 hours transcribed with a speech model, a team of research assistants trained to correct it, a segmentation model fine-tuned on 5,000 hand-coded utterances at 96.8% holdout agreement. The topic (empathy) is gone. The mechanics are what transfer.

The general rule I landed on, after reading more career-office guidance than I would like to admit: a resume bullet is a verb, a thing, a scale or tool, and a result. If it does not end with a number or a consequence, it is a responsibility, and nobody hires for responsibilities.

Titles are for the reader, not the registrar

“PhD Student, Graduate Research Fellow” is what the university called me. It is also nearly meaningless to someone who has never been inside a psychology department. The resume now says “Research Scientist and Statistics Instructor (Graduate Research Fellow),” with the official title in parentheses where a background check can find it. Same job, described for the person reading.

Publications became one line

Two peer-reviewed articles and eight conference presentations occupied a page of the CV. They are one line on the resume, with a Google Scholar link. Industry readers do not weigh a publication list; they weigh whether the work was used. So the feedback experiment became a bullet about preregistered replication standards, and the papers moved to the bottom.

Numbers must agree everywhere

The most useful thing I did was keep a single master file with every number and its source. The analytic sample for the suspension study is 6,351, not the 17,000 records I had access to. The tweet corpus was 7.8 million collected and 5.5 million analyzed in 2023, and 8.6 million analyzed in the 2026 rebuild; the resume and this site had better say the same thing. A recruiter who spots one drifting number stops believing the rest.

What hurt

Cutting the teaching. Thirteen terms of instruction compressed to one bullet, and the courses I was proudest of are not named. Cutting the theatre degree to half a line. Cutting the dog from the summary (he is back on the About page). None of it was wrong to cut; the page is for the reader.

The rules, in one place

Rebuild from the job, do not trim the CV. One master file, every number sourced. Verb, thing, scale, result. Titles the reader understands. Publications as a count and a link. Tools named only where they were actually used. One page for analyst roles, two for research-scientist roles, never a page and a quarter. And a plain-text paste test before sending, because a two-column template looks fine and parses as soup.
